title: shooting inquest report - Winnipeg Free Press
subtitle: Breaking News, Sports, Manitoba, Canada
article: This article was published 08/08/2018 (2580 days ago), so information in it may no longer be current.
No recommendations have resulted from a Winnipeg police-shooting inquest that took 10 years to get underway.

In a report released Wednesday from the inquest into the December 2007 death of Roy Thomas Bell, provincial court Judge Dale Schille wrote he didn't have any recommendations on how to prevent similar deaths in the future - due in large part to the delay in beginning the mandatory posthumous court process.

Police use-of-force policies have already been scrutinized and reviewed, and previous inquests have already made recommendations about them, Schille wrote in his report following the three-month inquest, which ended in March.

"The primary goal of any inquest is to generate recommendations that might later be implemented to prevent similar deaths in the future. The primary purpose of the inquest is significantly undermined if helpful recommendations are significantly delayed," he wrote.
Bell, who worked for the military for 231⁄2 years, was shot by police after officers were called to investigate a disturbance outside a Langside Street apartment Dec. 17, 2007.

He had been medically discharged from the military because of post-traumatic stress disorder, and had been diagnosed with depression and anxiety before he armed himself with a baseball bat and threatened a friend who had reportedly offended him with a comment about the military two days earlier.

Police were informed about Bell's mental-health issues when they responded to the call, and Bell's friends had been receiving threatening text messages from him before he stood outside their apartment building, wielding the bat and yelling.
Police arrived on scene just before 11 p.m., and informed the communications centre they were dealing with a man armed with a baseball bat. Thirty-four seconds later, Bell was shot dead.

Winnipeg Police Service Const. Wesley Johnson shot Bell five times, after Bell charged at Johnson and Const. Saif Khan. Khan had previously tried to use a Taser electro-shock weapon on Bell, but the probes didn't properly attach to the man's winter clothes, the inquest found.
The officers didn't call for backup after arriving on scene. When Khan testified at the inquest, he acknowledged he would have called for backup if he could go back in time.
"In my view, the failure to call for backup is not reflective of any systemic WPS issue that could be addressed through a recommendation issued in this report," Schille wrote.
After the shooting, the officers found a handgun on the ground near where Bell collapsed. The shooting was ruled justified after an internal WPS review (also reviewed by the Calgary Police Service).

Because Bell died at the hands of police, the inquest was mandatory, but protocol dictated it couldn't be called until the Crown's office decided no criminal charges would be laid, which delayed the process.
In this case, the chief medical examiner broke protocol by calling for the inquest in January 2015, before a final decision was made about criminal charges.
